overview: At 1279, this atlas stretches the name “Pagan” across a shape so large it covers Bagan, Ava, Pegu, Mrauk U, Chittagong and Mong Mao. History was far messier, and much more interesting. The old Pagan kingdom was already cracking under war, court rivalry and the rise of commanders near the rice-rich Kyaukse fields. Its king was deposed in 1297. Myinsaing, Pinya and Sagaing followed; Ava rose upstream in 1364, while Hanthawaddy-Pegu grew around the southern maritime world. Bagan itself did not vanish. Pilgrims, monks, potters, farmers and donors kept using its sacred landscape even after royal power moved elsewhere. Across this era, people dug channels and wells, fired green-glazed bowls, fed famine victims, copied books, painted familiar clothes into Buddhist stories and sent monks by ship to Sri Lanka. The atlas’s 1492 cutoff is another database seam, not the ending of one giant empire. This card follows the mapped interval while giving every successor its own name, and letting a cracked jar speak as loudly as a crown.

periods.title: The last Pagan court and a broken realm
periods.summary: Mongol pressure deepened a political crisis, but the invaders did not simply occupy and erase Bagan. Provincial commanders and regional courts gained the practical power that the old capital was losing.

periods.title: Myinsaing takes effective control
periods.summary: Kyawswa was deposed in 1297. The Myinsaing brothers held the Kyaukse granary zone, survived the 1301 Mongol siege, and ruled while a reduced Pagan kingship lingered in name.

periods.title: Pinya and Sagaing share the stage
periods.summary: Thihathu established Pinya, and a rival center developed at Sagaing. Inscriptions from rulers, officials and their families preserve political and religious life better than ordinary voices.

periods.title: Ava rises upstream; Pegu rules downstream
periods.summary: Ava formed in the irrigated upper country while Hanthawaddy-Pegu developed around the maritime delta. Their rivalry and exchange replaced any single continuous “Pagan” state.

periods.title: Several capitals, no single Pagan empire
periods.summary: Ava flourished inland, Pegu prospered toward the sea, and Mrauk U grew in the west. Bagan remained sacred and inhabited, but it was no longer the imperial capital.

periods.title: Dhammazedi’s Buddhist and maritime Pegu
periods.summary: The former monk Dhammazedi sponsored ordination reform, inscriptions and sacred construction while Pegu used coastal connections reaching Sri Lanka and the Indian Ocean.

sections.title: First, inspect the giant atlas umbrella

items.text: At 1279 the exact id is one Polygon with 72 coordinate positions and bounds from about 91.41°E to 101.01°E and 15.68°N to 25.98°N. Point tests place Bagan, Myinsaing, Ava, Pegu, Mrauk U, Chittagong and Mong Mao inside. That enormous result is display geometry, not one measured frontier.

The 1300 geometry is byte-for-byte the same as 1279, with SHA-256 e35027568fbae9667c146ca1904f4fa442f45033f58e65fae3b4fe19ecfbab0e. Yet Pagan’s king had already been deposed in 1297 and Myinsaing held effective power. A single frozen polygon cannot turn that political change back into a continuous empire.

The 1400 Polygon still has 72 positions and contains the same audited centers. Only tiny latitude changes produce hash 4bdfa26ae5d77ae0aabe3828d71aa923b7f3e7e2d1b7917025cb3a56b3dc2c47. By then Ava and Pegu were distinct powers. The outline is therefore a broad imported umbrella, not a snapshot of documented Pagan sovereignty.

The exact target disappears at 1492 and remains absent in 1500, while a separate pegu feature begins at 1492. That seam belongs to the atlas database. It does not mean Pegu suddenly appeared, and it does not mean a Pagan kingdom survived intact until someone changed the map label.

Three nearby names must stay separate: pagan is indexed 900 to 1100, bagan 1200 to 1279, and pagan-1279 1279 to 1492. The target is absent in 1100 and 1200 and had no card before this packet. This bundle adds no appliesTo aliases, so earlier cards and later Pegu keep their own identities.

sections.title: How a famous kingdom actually came apart

items.text: The Mongol incursions mattered, but the simple tale “Mongols sacked Bagan and ended everything in 1287” overstates the evidence. Richard Cooler notes that the forces probably penetrated northern Burma without capturing or occupying the capital. The deeper result was weakened central government and stronger provincial commanders.

Kyawswa gained Mongol recognition in 1297, but the Myinsaing brothers removed him that year; a Burmese inscription dates his dethronement ceremony to 17 December. This is why the card records 1297 as Pagan’s conventional political endpoint, even though a reduced royal line and the city continued.

Mongol troops began besieging Myinsaing on 25 January 1301 and withdrew on 6 April without capturing it. The brothers’ base stood beside the productive Kyaukse fields, making it strategically and economically strong. Survival came from defended resources and politics, not a magically invincible wall.

Thihathu established a new capital at Pinya in 1313, while Sagaing became a rival center across the river. In 1364 Ava began another political chapter. Scholars group 1287 to 1364 as the Myinsaing, Sagaing and Pinya period and 1364 onward as Ava; none of those names is a spelling variant of “Pagan.”

Surviving inscriptions were usually commissioned by rulers, officials and their families for religious donations. They are precious, but they tilt our view toward people wealthy enough to carve stone. A careful history therefore separates what these records say from what they leave dim: most farmers, craftspeople, children and household arguments.

sections.title: Ava, Pegu and other powers under one wrong label

items.text: Ava sat near the confluence of the Ayeyarwady and Myitnge rivers, beside access to Kyaukse’s irrigated rice zone. That location helped an inland court command food and transport. Pegu, farther downstream, grew in a maritime commercial setting. Geography shaped two different political economies inside the atlas’s single painted shape.

Fifteenth-century Ava presented itself as an heir to Pagan, but inheritance is not identity. It rebuilt networks of rule in Upper Myanmar and used older Buddhist and royal models. Pegu followed its own path in Lower Myanmar. Calling both “Pagan” erases the choices, rivalries and alliances that made the period historically interesting.

The imported polygon even includes Mrauk U and Chittagong in the west and Mong Mao in the northeast. Those point tests expose its scale; they do not make these places provinces of Pagan, Ava or Pegu. The shape is useful for finding a region on screen and unsafe for measuring medieval control.

Court chronicles and royal inscriptions can make history look like a parade of wars and donations. Hla Pe’s source survey shows why caution matters: surviving stone texts are often religious dedications by rulers and officials. They illuminate elite choices while leaving much ordinary work, family life and disagreement unwritten.

A chronology can be exact without pretending borders were. This card follows the atlas continuously from 1279 to 1492, but its periods change names when power changes: late Pagan, Myinsaing, Pinya and Sagaing, then Ava and Hanthawaddy-Pegu. Mrauk U and other centers remain neighbors with their own histories.

sections.title: Buddhist institutions, books and royal ambition

items.text: Bagan did not become a ghost city when the court moved away. UNESCO describes a living sacred landscape where worship, merit-making, farming and communities continued among thousands of monuments. A monastery or temple could remain a place of devotion and local memory long after the imperial court stopped directing the region.

A 1442 four-sided stone at Pagan records a monastery founded by a local lord related to Ava’s king and his consort, a former king’s daughter. The consort sold her hair to help buy a Tipiṭaka and other texts. This vivid act ties family strategy, devotion and a working library together.

The same donation included lands and enslaved people as well as books. That inequality belongs in the story: monuments and libraries could be supported by people whose labor and freedom were controlled by elites. Admiring a manuscript’s learning should not make the attached human cost disappear from the page.

Dhammazedi sent twenty-two senior monks toward Sri Lanka to receive Mahāvihāra ordination and establish that lineage in his realm. The project used ships, letters, gifts, port contacts and royal money. Religious reform was therefore both spiritual and organizational, connecting Lower Myanmar to an Indian Ocean Buddhist network.

The Kalyānī stones were also arguments for royal power. Three carried Pali and the others a Mon version with more local detail. Dhammazedi’s court used durable stone, learned languages and authorized ritual boundaries to define a disciplined monastic community. The monument tells us what reformers wanted, not that every monk agreed.

sections.title: Fields, water and what reached the bowl

items.text: Kyaukse’s irrigated fields were the chief granary of central Burma, which helps explain why the Myinsaing rulers based nearby became powerful. Canals and carefully managed water turned the dry zone into dependable rice country. Control of food-producing land could matter more than possession of an old ceremonial capital.

A 1375 inscription tells of a widow responding to hunger: she gave cooked food to thirty-seven monks, uncooked supplies to two hundred more, and twice daily cooked fifty khwak of rice for starving people. It records charitable action during hardship, not a normal household menu or proof that relief reached everyone.

Land transactions could be marked by feasts involving ox, pig and liquor, while records supplied monks with rice and curry for morning and evening meals. These are specific inscriptional scenes, not a universal diet. They show that food joined law, religion and hospitality, and that medieval paperwork could arrive with dinner.

At Otein Taung, a pottery village supplied Bagan’s fourteenth-century inhabitants with household utensils, roof tiles and well linings. A well lining helps manage access to groundwater, but it does not prove that the water was germ-free or equally available. Archaeology here supports containers and infrastructure more firmly than public-health claims.

Bagan’s domestic archaeology remains preliminary. Pottery studies can classify vessels, standardization and production choices more securely than recipes, portions or who ate first. A bowl proves that somebody made and used a container; it cannot identify every ingredient or tell us whose hand reached it first.

sections.title: Families, rank, care and unequal choices

items.text: The 1442 donor couple belonged to the royal world: he was a local lord and nephew of Ava’s reigning king; she was the daughter of an earlier king. Their joint project shows a married elite household acting politically and religiously. It cannot stand in for the routines of farming families.

An Old Mon inscriptional chronology records Queen Shin Sawbu donating land in 1455 and sharing repair work with Dhammazedi in 1469. A ruling woman could direct property and religious patronage, yet royal evidence cannot tell us how much choice ordinary women had in work, marriage or household decisions.

The 1442 monastery record joins royal relatives, monks, learned readers, land and enslaved labor in one donation. It reveals a steep social world in which elite merit-making depended on controlled property and people. It does not supply a neat class ladder, a typical family size or the workers’ own voices.

Dhammazedi’s rules required checking novice and ordination candidates and threatened penalties involving candidates’ parents, relatives or donors when procedures were ignored. Families and patrons could therefore be entangled in a young man’s monastic path. The rule describes institutional expectations, not every family’s private feelings.

Medical-history sources record learned texts more clearly than bedside routines. We do not know how most sick children, elderly farmers or injured potters were treated at home, who paid, or who decided. Family help is plausible, but the reviewed sources do not let us map it.

sections.title: Homes, clothes, work and clever hands

items.text: Ordinary houses are frustratingly faint in the evidence. Bagan archaeology is rich in brick religious monuments but has rarely targeted habitation, while Otein Taung yields roof tiles, utensils and well linings for fourteenth-century residents. These objects show equipped homes without giving us a trustworthy standard floor plan.

Art historians use Ava-period religious paintings cautiously: local settings include architecture, hairstyles, jewelry and dress marked by station, along with commoners fishing, plowing and making pots. A painted Jātaka is not a candid photograph, but selected details can preserve how artists made sacred stories look familiar.

Shwe Creek pottery analysis found strong standardization among utilitarian wares and considers both attached production for elites and independent market production. Standard rims suggest practiced hands and repeated expectations. Still, the study is preliminary, so one sherd cannot tell us whether its maker worked freely, for a patron or both over time.

A heavy glazed jar found at Myaung Mya bears a Myanmar-script date equivalent to 1362. Nearby kilns differed in shape, and circular platforms and rollers served as firing supports. A kiln “failure” can be a historian’s success: wasters and furniture preserve the steps that a perfect finished pot hides.

Fifteenth-century Twante kilns used brick, columnar supports and pointed fireboxes. Potters made green-glazed plates, bowls, jars, bottles, tiles and animal figures, supporting vessels on tubular pontils during firing. The excavated kilns are not directly dated, so the publication calls their fifteenth-century attribution strong but circumstantial.

sections.title: Learning, medicine, leisure and a stone voice

items.text: Dhammazedi ordered that novice candidates first practice writing letters and learn the refuges and precepts. This is direct evidence for literacy training inside a monastic pathway. It does not prove a village school for every child, equal access for girls, or a single age at which boys began learning.

The 1442 Pagan library held hundreds of works on Buddhist teaching, grammar, dictionaries, poetics, meter, medicine, worldly wisdom, astrology and tantra. Scholar monks and other people “of good birth” were expected to study them. The range is dazzling; access was selective, and book ownership is not the same as mass literacy.

Medical treatises appear in that Ava-era book record, and a government historical survey also notes medicinal and astronomical works on the monastery stone. This proves learned medicine circulated. It does not identify a standard remedy, diagnosis, healer’s training, hospital, survival rate or ordinary family’s access, so those details remain unknown.

Poetics shows that learned people studied how language could sound and persuade; paintings add music, court scenes and lively work. The reviewed target-period sources do not securely name children’s games. Better to leave play partly blank than hand medieval children a modern toy by accident.

The authentic short sample from Dhammazedi’s 1476 Kalyānī inscription is “နမော တဿ ဘဂဝတော အရဟတော သမ္မာသမ္ဗုဒ္ဓဿ။” Transliteration: “Namo tassa Bhagavato arahato Sammāsambuddhassa.” Translation: “Reverence to the Blessed One, the Holy One, the Fully Enlightened One.” This is Pali in a normalized modern Myanmar-script rendering, not a facsimile of fifteenth-century letterforms.

sections.title: Trade, technology and ideas on the move

items.text: Ava-era trade drew overseas merchants seeking precious stones, lac, ivory, horn, lead, tin and large Martaban jars, often exchanging Indian textiles. Cotton and silk also moved overland toward China. These lists spotlight valued goods; behind them stood miners, growers, potters, pack handlers, boat crews and brokers whom the catalogue rarely names.

Twante sat by waterways that made bulky pottery easier to ship. Fifteenth- and sixteenth-century sherds line the canal, and chemically matched celadon reached the Persian Gulf; a 1450 to 1487 Philippine wreck carried at least one Burmese plate. A bowl could travel farther than most of the people who made it.

Glaze technology changed by region rather than marching in one straight line. The 1362 Myaung Mya jar, varied kiln forms and fifteenth-century Mrauk U tiles and domestic wares show experimentation across several centers. “Made in medieval Myanmar” therefore covers multiple workshops, clays, firing choices and political settings.

Pegu’s maritime links carried more than cargo. Dhammazedi’s embassy used established merchant and port relationships to reach Sri Lanka, exchange gifts and renew an ordination lineage. Monks, letters and ritual rules traveled alongside trade. Ocean connections helped a delta kingdom build both authority and a learned religious network.

Ava art did not simply copy Pagan. By the late fourteenth century sculptors developed broader-faced Buddha images and increasingly favored marble; painters adapted older religious subjects into local settings. Technical continuity and invention worked together, which is a more accurate achievement story than awarding every later object to a vanished Pagan court.

sections.title: Water, toilets, health and what we cannot know

items.text: Rivers, irrigation and wells served different jobs. The Ayeyarwady carried people and goods; Kyaukse channels supported rice; Bagan well linings reached groundwater. None of this by itself proves clean drinking water or equal access. Water engineering can be impressive while still leaving disease, maintenance and household collection mostly invisible.

At Old Bagan, stacked earthenware tubes were interpreted by archaeology staff as possible latrine linings, and similar fragments appeared at Otein Taung. The report says “thought” rather than proven, and it does not securely date those installations to 1279 to 1492. They are a cautious clue, not a royal flush of certainty.

No reviewed excavation securely identifies a target-period toilet, cesspit, household drain or citywide sewer. Well linings are not latrines, and a possible latrine tube does not establish plumbing. People certainly managed bodily waste somehow, but the design, users, cleaning labor and health effects remain unknown in this evidence set.

Texts on medicine show organized knowledge, but they do not tell us what happened when an ordinary child had fever or a potter cut a hand. Ritual support, family care, plant remedies and specialist treatment may all have mattered; this packet cannot rank them or attach a success rate without inventing evidence.

Earthquakes and warfare damaged fields, buildings and food security. Inscriptions record repair work after a 1372 earthquake and starvation in 1375, showing that health depended on harvests and shelter as well as learned medicine. Recovery involved patrons, workers, monks and cooks, social infrastructure long before anyone used that phrase.

ending.text: Pagan’s unified royal state ended conventionally in 1297, but neither Bagan nor the people inside this oversized polygon ended with it. Political power moved through Myinsaing, Pinya, Sagaing, Ava, Hanthawaddy-Pegu and other centers. Bagan remained a layered sacred place where worship, merit-making, farming and community life continued. UNESCO now records 3,595 monuments within a living landscape, a reminder that continuity belongs to practices and people as well as dynastic names. The atlas stops pagan-1279 in 1492 and starts a separate Pegu feature, but that database handoff is not a mass migration, sudden religious break or single historical conquest.
